parts: Advertising is the activity of presenting a sponsored message about a product, service or idea to prospective customers to make them aware of it and induce them to buy. The American Marketing Association defines it as 'any paid form of non-personal presentation and promotion of ideas, goods and services by an identified sponsor'. The firm that pays is the sponsor or advertiser; the message is the advertisement; the newspaper, TV or hoarding that carries it is the medium. DAGMAR (Defining Advertising Goals for Measured Advertising Results) is a method of setting and measuring advertising goals.

(1) Non-personal — no face-to-face contact; addressed to people in general (mass communication). (2) Paid form of communication — the sponsor pays for space or time. (3) Promotion of a product, service or idea. (4) Identified sponsor — the advertiser's name is always disclosed. (5) Communicated through media. (6) It aims to inform and persuade. Advertising is a powerful communication force and an important part of the promotion mix (with personal selling, sales promotion and publicity). It is not flexible — once fixed, the message cannot be changed to suit each customer.

(1) Educating customers about products and their uses (Tata Namak with iodine). (2) Creating demand for new products (gel pens). (3) Retaining existing customers and maintaining demand by reminding them (Nirma). (4) Increasing sales of existing as well as new products. (5) Assisting salesmen — customers already know the product's features. (6) Helping mass production and lowering costs; building the image of the firm; facing competition. For society it creates employment and supports newspapers and TV.

Print media — newspapers and periodicals (press advertising). Newspapers: wide circulation, low cost, can be repeated daily, flexible (changes at short notice), available in many languages for regional markets; but short life, read casually, useless for illiterates. Best for consumer goods for the general public, new launches, clearance sales and exchange offers; a local edition suits local businesses such as a coaching institute. Periodicals (weekly, monthly magazines — India Today, Femina, Reader's Digest): longer life than newspapers, selective readership (Femina for women's products such as sarees and herbal cosmetics), good printing; but costlier, smaller reach, less flexible.

Electronic media — radio, television, Internet. Radio: heard regularly, reaches illiterates and people in remote areas, can be heard while travelling or working; but no visual impact and easily forgotten. Television: most effective because it has audio-visual impact; products can be demonstrated; slogans and celebrities have lasting impact; wide choice of channels; reaches illiterates — but costly to make and telecast, and viewers switch channels in breaks. Internet: information from all over the world within a fraction of a second, available any time; but needs a computer or phone and skill, not for illiterates.

Other (outdoor) media — hoardings (large boards painted or electronically designed, visible day and night), posters (on walls and bridges), vehicular or transit displays (advertisements on buses and trains, which carry the message to many people), gift items, neon signs. The choice of medium depends on the nature of the product, the target customers, the funds available and the space and time available. For the blind, radio is the medium; for illiterates, radio, television and cinema.
